title: Longest Common Subsequence
directAnswer: Find the length of the longest subsequence common to two strings (characters in order, not necessarily contiguous). Compare the strings character by character: when two characters match, take the diagonal +1; when they don't, take the better of dropping one character from either string. That's the canonical 2D DP — dp[i][j] = match ? dp[i-1][j-1]+1 : max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — in O(m·n) time.

rules: State is **(prefix of A, prefix of B)** — `dp[i][j]` is the LCS of the first `i` chars of A and first `j` of B.
On a **match**, jump to the diagonal `dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`: both characters are consumed and contribute 1.
On a **mismatch**, take `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])` — you must drop a character from one string, so try both and keep the better.
Use a **(m+1)×(n+1)** table with row 0 and column 0 as zeros: an empty string shares nothing, the natural base case.
Subsequence ≠ substring — characters must keep order but **need not be contiguous**, which is exactly why the 'skip a char' branch exists.
whenToUse: Two sequences (strings/arrays) and you're aligning, matching, or editing one into the other
Answer depends on comparing a prefix of one input against a prefix of the other
'Longest common', 'edit distance', 'minimum deletions to make equal' style phrasing
Order matters but contiguity does not — the hallmark of subsequence DP
antiSignals: Need a contiguous match → that's Longest Common *Substring* (reset to 0 on mismatch)
Only one sequence → likely a 1D DP (LIS, House Robber), not a 2D grid
You need the actual subsequence string, not just its length → still DP but add a backtrack pass
Sequences are huge and only length matters → consider Hirschberg's O(n) space, not full table
remember.takeaway: LCS is the archetype of two-string DP: index into both strings, branch on match vs mismatch, and the recurrence falls out. Once you see the prefix-vs-prefix grid, Edit Distance, Shortest Common Supersequence, and Delete Operation for Two Strings are all the same machine with a different per-cell formula.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can model a problem over *two* inputs as a 2D DP — define dp[i][j] over prefixes, get the match/mismatch transition right, and reason about why the diagonal represents 'both characters used'.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Confusing subsequence with substring (resetting to 0 on a mismatch), or mixing up the 1-based DP indices with the 0-based string indices and reading the wrong characters.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the recurrence from the brute-force recursion first, then mention you can roll the table to two rows for O(min(m,n)) space, and note the same grid solves Edit Distance with a tweaked transition.

problemStatement:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their **longest common subsequence**. If there is no common subsequence, return `0`.

A **subsequence** of a string is a new string generated from the original string with some characters (can be none) deleted ***without changing the relative order*** of the remaining characters.

A **common subsequence** of two strings is a subsequence that is common to both strings.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of lowercase English characters only
Order of characters must be preserved (subsequence, not subset)
understanding: Given two strings, find how many characters you can pick from both — in the same relative order in each — such that the picked characters are identical. You're not looking for a contiguous block; gaps are allowed as long as order is preserved.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Subsequence or substring — do the characters have to be contiguous?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Subsequence: order must be preserved but the characters need not be adjacent. 'ace' is a subsequence of 'abcde'. This is the crux of the problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the length or the actual subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the length for LeetCode 1143. Reconstructing the string is a common follow-up and needs an extra backtrack over the table.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the strings be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraints say length ≥ 1, but the DP base case (an empty prefix shares nothing) handles length 0 gracefully — return 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the matching case-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — only lowercase letters appear, so 'a' and 'A' never collide here, but in general you'd clarify casing.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both approaches model the same recurrence; the table just memoises what the recursion recomputes.

approaches.name: Plain Recursion — Compare from the Ends
approaches.whenToMention: Use it to derive the recurrence out loud, then immediately call out that it's exponential and needs memoisation. Never present it as the final answer.
hints: Look at the last character of each string. If they're equal, that character can be part of the LCS — what's left to solve?
If the last characters differ, at least one of them isn't in the LCS. Try dropping the last char of A, then of B, and keep the better result.
Write lcs(i, j) over prefixes: match → 1 + lcs(i-1, j-1); mismatch → max(lcs(i-1, j), lcs(i, j-1)); empty prefix → 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each mismatch spawns two recursive calls and the recursion depth is up to m+n, so without memoisation the call tree is exponential. The only memory is the recursion stack, O(m+n) deep.
approaches.explanation:
Define `lcs(i, j)` as the LCS length of `text1[0..i-1]` and `text2[0..j-1]`. Decide one character at a time, working from the back of each string.

**Why we look at the ends.** Consider the *last* characters of the two prefixes. If they're equal, then there's an optimal LCS that *uses* this matched pair: pair them up, add 1, and recurse on the strings with both last characters removed — `1 + lcs(i-1, j-1)`. If they differ, that pair can't both be in the LCS, so at least one of those two characters is useless — we try removing the last char of the first string (`lcs(i-1, j)`) and removing the last char of the second (`lcs(i, j-1)`), and keep whichever yields more.

**Why an empty prefix returns 0.** If either string has run out of characters, there's nothing left to match, so the LCS is length 0. That's the recursion's base case and the source of the table's zero row/column later.

**Why we don't ship this.** The mismatch branch forks into two subproblems, and those subproblems overlap massively — `lcs(i-1, j)` and `lcs(i, j-1)` both eventually call `lcs(i-1, j-1)`. Recomputing the same `(i, j)` pair over and over makes the naive tree exponential. The fix is to *remember* each `(i, j)` result once computed — which turns this exact recurrence into the O(m·n) DP below.
approaches.insight: The whole problem hinges on one decision repeated: 'do the current ends match?' Match collapses both strings by one (the diagonal move); mismatch advances one string only (a horizontal or vertical move). Seeing the recursion as movement on a grid is the bridge to the table — the table is literally the memo of this function.

pitfalls: Indexing the strings with i and j directly instead of i-1 / j-1 — off-by-one and out-of-bounds.
Resetting to 0 on a mismatch (that's substring logic) instead of taking the max of the two skips.
Presenting this as a final solution — without memoisation it TLEs on length-1000 inputs.

approaches.name: 2D DP Table — Bottom-Up Prefix Grid (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'memoise the recursion into a (m+1)×(n+1) grid and fill it bottom-up.'
hints: Take the recursive lcs(i, j) and store every answer in a table indexed by (i, j) so you never recompute a pair.
Make the table (m+1)×(n+1) so row 0 and column 0 represent empty prefixes and are all zeros — the base case baked in.
Fill it in increasing i, j. Each cell uses the diagonal (on a match) or the cell above/left (on a mismatch), all already computed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are (m+1)·(n+1) cells and each is filled in O(1) from three neighbours, so time is O(m·n). The full table is stored, so space is O(m·n) — reducible to O(min(m,n)) by keeping two rows.
approaches.explanation:
Allocate `dp[m+1][n+1]` where `dp[i][j]` is the LCS length of the first `i` characters of `text1` and the first `j` of `text2`. Row 0 and column 0 are all zeros (empty prefix). Fill the rest in increasing order of `i` and `j`.

**Why the table mirrors the recursion exactly.** Each cell answers the same question `lcs(i, j)` did — but because we fill in increasing `i, j`, every value the recurrence needs (`dp[i-1][j-1]`, `dp[i-1][j]`, `dp[i][j-1]`) is already sitting in the table. So the exponential blow-up disappears: each `(i, j)` pair is computed once. The table *is* the memo.

**Why the diagonal means 'match'.** When `text1[i-1] == text2[j-1]`, we extend the best alignment of the two shorter prefixes by this matched pair: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1`. The diagonal cell represents 'both strings one character shorter', so adding 1 records that we consumed a character from each and gained a match.

**Why the mismatch takes a max of above and left.** If the current characters differ, the LCS can't use both, so we must skip one: `dp[i-1][j]` is 'ignore `text1`'s current char', `dp[i][j-1]` is 'ignore `text2`'s'. We keep the larger — exactly the recursion's mismatch branch, now read from already-filled neighbours.

**Why the indices are offset by one.** The `+1` table dimension lets row/column 0 be the empty-prefix base case without special-casing, which is why we compare `text1[i-1]` against `text2[j-1]` — table index `i` corresponds to string index `i-1`. The answer lives at `dp[m][n]`.
approaches.insight: The deep idea is that a two-input problem becomes a *plane* of subproblems, and filling that plane in dependency order replaces recursion with three array reads. Internalise the cell picture — diagonal-plus-one on a match, max-of-neighbours on a mismatch — and Edit Distance, Delete Operation, and Shortest Common Supersequence are all the same grid with a different per-cell rule.

pitfalls: Sizing the table m×n instead of (m+1)×(n+1) — you lose the zero base row/column and mishandle the first characters.
Treating a mismatch like a substring problem and resetting dp[i][j] to 0 — that computes longest common *substring*.
Reading dp[i][j] off the diagonal on a mismatch — only matches use the diagonal.

commonMistakes: Confusing subsequence with substring — resetting the cell to 0 on a mismatch instead of taking max(up, left).
Mixing the 1-based DP indices with 0-based string indices and comparing the wrong characters.
Forgetting the (m+1)×(n+1) zero border, so the first row/column of the recurrence reads garbage.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Substring reset on mismatch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Resetting dp[i][j] to 0 when characters differ computes the longest common *contiguous* substring, not the subsequence — a different and smaller answer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one between table and string indices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Table cell dp[i][j] covers prefixes of length i and j, so the characters being compared are at string indices i-1 and j-1, not i and j.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Naive recursion without memoisation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The mismatch branch forks into two overlapping subproblems; recomputing them is exponential and TLEs on length-1000 strings.

followupVariations.title: Edit Distance
followupVariations.hint: Same prefix grid; on a mismatch take 1 + min(insert, delete, replace) instead of a plain max.

followupVariations.title: Delete Operation for Two Strings
followupVariations.hint: Answer is m + n − 2·LCS — the chars outside the LCS must be deleted from each side.

followupVariations.title: Shortest Common Supersequence
followupVariations.hint: Build the LCS table, then walk it backwards to weave both strings around the shared subsequence.

followupVariations.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
followupVariations.hint: It's LCS of the string with its own reverse — the same table, one input reversed.

patternNote: Canonical two-string 2D DP — index over prefixes of both inputs, branch on match (diagonal + 1) vs mismatch (max of neighbours). Recognise it for any 'align / edit / longest common' question over two sequences; Edit Distance, Shortest Common Supersequence, and Longest Palindromic Subsequence are the same grid with a tweaked per-cell rule.
